nodes.PRODUCERS: In the simple view, industries and the markets for their products are one node. Money comes in when households, governments, investors and foreign buyers pay for goods and services. It goes out as wages, mixed income and operating surplus, as taxes on products and production, and as payments for imports. What producers pay each other for inputs, and the traders' and transporters' margins, circulate inside this node: they are listed here, not drawn.
nodes.GOV: In the top-flows view, the tax accounts, the Centre and the States are one node, because most long annual series cover general government as a whole. Transfers between the Centre and the States (devolution and grants) and the individual tax heads are listed inside it.
nodes.PRDS: Each product account collects what buyers pay for that product: households, industries buying inputs, governments, investors and foreign buyers. It then pays the industries that made the product (at basic prices), foreign suppliers for imports, taxes on products, and the trade and transport margin. Product subsidies are negative taxes, so they show as reversed flows into these markets. The node is drawn twice: on the left as the seller, on the right as where spending arrives.
nodes.PROD: Industries receive the value of what they produce from the product markets. They pay for inputs bought from other industries (intermediate consumption), wages, the mixed income of the self-employed, gross operating surplus (profits, rents and depreciation), and taxes on production net of production subsidies. Output less inputs is gross value added. The government's own services, such as administration, schools and hospitals, are industries too.
nodes.ROW: India's current account with the rest of the world. Foreigners pay India for exports and pay incomes and transfers, such as remittances, interest and dividends, to Indian residents. India pays them for imports and pays incomes and transfers abroad. What the rest of the world earns from India and does not spend here is its saving in India, which equals India's current-account deficit. It flows on to Saving and investment, where it is matched by foreign investment and lending.
nodes.FACT: Factor accounts collect what industries pay for work and capital: compensation of employees (regular and casual), the mixed income of household enterprises such as farms and small shops, and gross operating surplus, which includes profits, rents and depreciation. They pass this income on to its owners: households, companies, financial firms and governments. A little pay crosses the border in each direction.
nodes.HH: Households receive wages, mixed income, rent (including the rent owner-occupiers are deemed to pay themselves), interest and dividends, pensions, cash transfers and remittances. They spend on consumption, pay income tax, interest and insurance premiums, and send money abroad; what is left is their saving. Non-profit institutions serving households (NPISH) are inside this account. The split into ten groups, rural and urban fifths ranked by monthly spending per person (MPCE), is estimated. The household residual that national accounts publish but cannot allocate is shown separately, under Discrepancies.
nodes.NFC: Non-financial companies, public and private. They receive their operating surplus and some interest, dividends and insurance claims. They pay interest, dividends, corporation tax, royalties and income to foreign investors; what is left is their gross saving, which funds their investment. How property income is split between companies and other sectors is estimated, partly with the old-base national-accounts structure.
nodes.FC: Financial corporations: the RBI, banks, NBFCs, and insurers and pension funds. Banks and NBFCs receive interest on loans and pay interest on deposits and borrowing; insurers and pension funds collect premiums and pay claims and investment income to policyholders and members; the RBI earns on its reserves and transfers its surplus to the Centre. The financial sector's total saving follows national accounts; the split among the four types is estimated. Mutual funds appear only in Saving and investment.
nodes.TAX: Each tax account collects one kind of tax from those who pay it and passes it to the government that keeps it: GST, customs, Union excise, State VAT and excise, other product taxes, production taxes, income tax and corporation tax. GST is recorded on a net basis, after the settlement of integrated GST between the Centre and the States, so there is no separate IGST account. Subsidies are negative taxes: governments pay into the subsidy accounts, which pay the product markets and industries, so those flows are drawn reversed.
nodes.CEN: The Union government, with its autonomous bodies and the Food Corporation of India. It receives its taxes, dividends from public enterprises, the RBI's surplus, and rents such as spectrum fees and petroleum royalties. It spends on public services (including free food grain), pays the States their share of taxes and grants, pays interest on its debt, pensions, cash transfers and subsidies. In the year shown its current spending exceeded its current receipts, so its gross saving was negative; its capital account covers the gap by borrowing. How general-government totals are split between the Centre and the States is estimated.
nodes.STA: State governments, Union Territories with legislatures, and local bodies. They receive State GST, VAT, excise, stamp duties and other own taxes, their share of Union taxes, grants from the Centre, and mining royalties. They spend on public services such as police, schools and hospitals, pay pensions, cash transfers, interest and subsidies, and save the rest. How general-government totals are split between the Centre and the States is estimated.
nodes.SI: Capital accounts. Each sector's capital account receives its gross saving and the money it raises by taking on liabilities, and pays for investment (buildings, machinery, inventories and valuables) and for the financial assets it acquires. The rest of the world's capital account holds India's current-account deficit and the foreign investment and lending that finance it. In the simple view the financial markets are folded in here, so the money that passes through them is internal to this node.
nodes.DISC: Official statistics publish some totals that do not quite add up. Instead of hiding these gaps, the map carries them in this account: the household residual (household disposable income less consumption less saving); the reconciliation between national accounts and the balance of payments on services imports, an accounting adjustment and not money paid abroad; the saving-investment errors and omissions, part of which is valuables that national accounts assign to no sector; and the GDP expenditure discrepancy, which is zero in 2023-24. Balancing never moved these items.
nodes.FINM: Each instrument account receives money from the sectors that acquire that asset, for example households placing deposits or banks buying government securities, and pays it to the sectors that take on the matching liability, for example banks accepting deposits or governments issuing bonds. Every market clears in the year: what is acquired equals what is incurred. These are flows during the year, not holdings. Who holds what from whom comes from RBI's flow of funds and is estimated; differences between national accounts and the flow of funds sit in the residual 'other accounts'. The map shows saving and borrowing meeting in the same markets in the same year; it pools the money, so it cannot trace which saver's rupee funded which borrower.
nodes.PRDS.AGRI: Markets for crops, livestock products, and forest and fish products: what households, food processors and exporters buy from farms, forests and fisheries.
nodes.PRDS.MINE: Markets for coal, crude oil, natural gas and other minerals, much of it bought as inputs by refineries, power plants and factories, and much of the crude oil imported.
nodes.PRDS.MANU: Markets for manufactured goods: processed food, textiles, fuels, chemicals, medicines, metals, machinery, electronics and vehicles. Most of India's imports land here.
nodes.PRDS.CNUT: Markets for construction work, which is mostly investment, and for electricity, gas and water.
nodes.PRDS.TTC: Markets for trade, hotel and restaurant, transport and communication services. Most of the trade and transport services are sold as margins on goods.
nodes.PRDS.FIRE: Markets for financial and insurance services, housing services (actual and imputed rent), real estate, business and IT services. IT services are a large export.
nodes.PRDS.PSOC: Markets for education, health, personal services, and public administration and defence. Governments are the main buyers of public administration, and pay for much of health and education.
nodes.PROD.AGRI: Farming, forestry and fishing industries. Most of their income is the mixed income of farm households.
nodes.PROD.MINE: Coal mining, oil and gas extraction and other mining. They pay royalties to governments.
nodes.PROD.MANU: Manufacturing industries, from food processing to vehicles. They buy most of their inputs from other industries and from imports.
nodes.PROD.CNUT: Construction, and electricity, gas and water supply.
nodes.PROD.TTC: Trade, hotels and restaurants, transport and storage, and communication.
nodes.PROD.FIRE: Banking, insurance, ownership of dwellings, real estate and business services, and IT services.
nodes.PROD.PSOC: Education, health, community and personal services, and public administration and defence.
nodes.FACT.LAB: Compensation of employees: wages and salaries of regular workers and of casual workers. The split between regular and casual pay comes from labour survey shares.
nodes.HH.RUR: Rural households in five groups (fifths of the rural population ranked by monthly spending per person). The split of national household totals across these groups is estimated.
nodes.HH.URB: Urban households in five groups (fifths of the urban population ranked by monthly spending per person). The split of national household totals across these groups is estimated.
nodes.TAX.GST: Central GST (with UTGST), State GST and the GST compensation cess, each after the settlement of integrated GST.
nodes.TAX.OIND: Customs duties, Union excise, State VAT and sales tax, State excise and other taxes on products.
nodes.TAX.DIR: Personal income tax (including securities transaction tax) and corporation tax.
nodes.SI.CORP: Capital accounts of public and private companies: their saving, investment, borrowing and financial assets.
nodes.SI.FIN: Capital accounts of the RBI, banks, NBFCs, insurers and pension funds, and mutual funds.
nodes.SI.GOV: Capital accounts of the Centre and the States: their saving (negative for the Centre in the year shown), investment, capital grants and borrowing.
nodes.FINM.MONEY: Currency and deposits, including NRI deposits.
nodes.FINM.GOVD: Government securities and treasury bills of the Centre and the States, and small savings schemes. The map pools Centre and State paper, so it cannot say who bought which.
nodes.FINM.SEC: Corporate bonds and commercial paper, shares, and mutual fund units.
nodes.FINM.OTH: Foreign-exchange reserves, and other accounts payable and receivable, which also hold the residuals that reconcile national accounts with the flow of funds.
nodes.A_CROP: Crop farming: its output is sold as crops; most of its income is farmers' mixed income.
nodes.A_LVST: Livestock farming: dairy, poultry and meat.
nodes.A_OILG: Crude petroleum and natural gas production.
nodes.A_OMIN: Mining and quarrying other than coal, oil and gas.
nodes.A_BVTB: Manufacture of beverages and tobacco products.
nodes.A_TXAP: Manufacture of textiles, apparel and leather goods.
nodes.A_WOOD: Manufacture of wood products, paper, printing and furniture.
nodes.A_GJOM: Gems and jewellery, and other manufacturing.
nodes.A_CHEM: Manufacture of chemicals, including fertilisers, and rubber and plastic products.
nodes.A_NMMN: Manufacture of cement and other non-metallic mineral products.
nodes.A_MTLS: Manufacture of basic metals: iron and steel and non-ferrous metals.
nodes.A_MACH: Fabricated metal products, machinery, and repair and installation.
nodes.A_TREQ: Motor vehicles and other transport equipment.
nodes.A_UTIL: Electricity, gas, water supply and other utility services.
nodes.A_TRAD: Wholesale and retail trade, and repair of motor vehicles. Most of its output is sold as margins on goods.
nodes.A_TRNS: Rail, road, water and air transport, transport support services and storage.
nodes.A_FINS: Banks, NBFCs and other financial services, as producers. Their output includes the margin they earn between loan and deposit rates (FISIM).
nodes.A_INSR: Insurance and pension providers, as producers of insurance services.
nodes.A_DWEL: Ownership of dwellings: the housing stock treated as an industry. Its output is rent, actual and imputed; its income is mostly the operating surplus of households that own homes.
nodes.A_BSRE: Real estate, legal, accounting, renting and other business services.
nodes.A_ITSV: Computer programming, consultancy and related services.
nodes.A_EDUC: Education and research, public and private.
nodes.A_HLTH: Human health and social work, public and private.
nodes.A_OSRV: Community, social, personal and other services.
nodes.A_PADM: Public administration and defence. Its output is valued at cost, and it is bought almost entirely by governments as government consumption.
nodes.C_CROP: Market for crops. Buyers include households, food processors and exporters.
nodes.C_LVST: Market for milk, eggs, meat and other livestock products.
nodes.C_FOFI: Market for forest products and fish.
nodes.C_COAL: Market for coal and lignite, mostly bought by power plants and steel makers.
nodes.C_OILG: Market for crude petroleum and natural gas, much of it imported.
nodes.C_OMIN: Market for metal ores and other minerals.
nodes.C_BVTB: Market for beverages and tobacco products, which carry heavy product taxes.
nodes.C_TXAP: Market for textiles, clothing, footwear and leather goods.
nodes.C_WOOD: Market for wood products, paper, printed matter and furniture.
nodes.C_GJOM: Market for gems, jewellery and other manufactures, including the gold and silver that households buy as valuables.
nodes.C_RPET: Market for petrol, diesel and other refined products. Union excise and State VAT on fuels are collected here.
nodes.C_CHEM: Market for chemicals, fertilisers, pesticides, rubber and plastics. The fertiliser subsidy lowers prices here.
nodes.C_NMMN: Market for cement, glass, ceramics and other non-metallic mineral products.
nodes.C_MTLS: Market for iron, steel and other basic metals.
nodes.C_MACH: Market for metal products, machinery and repair services.
nodes.C_ELEQ: Market for electronics and electrical equipment, a large share of it imported.
nodes.C_TREQ: Market for motor vehicles and other transport equipment. Motor-vehicle tax is collected here.
nodes.C_CNST: Market for construction work, almost all of it bought as investment.
nodes.C_UTIL: Market for electricity, gas and water.
nodes.C_TRAD: Market for trade and repair services. Most of it is supplied as the trade margin on goods.
nodes.C_TRNS: Market for transport and storage services, partly supplied as the transport margin on goods.
nodes.C_COMM: Market for telecom, postal and broadcasting services.
nodes.C_FINS: Market for financial services, including the interest margin banks earn (FISIM).
nodes.C_INSR: Market for insurance and pension services: the service charge, not the premiums themselves.
nodes.C_DWEL: Market for housing services: rent paid by tenants, the rent owner-occupiers are deemed to pay themselves, and government-provided housing.
nodes.C_BSRE: Market for real estate, legal, accounting and other business services.
nodes.C_ITSV: Market for software and IT services, a large export.
nodes.C_EDUC: Market for education and research services.
nodes.C_HLTH: Market for health and social care services.
nodes.C_OSRV: Market for personal, community and other services.
nodes.C_PADM: Market for public administration and defence services, bought by governments.
nodes.M_TTM: The margin account: what buyers pay traders and transporters to bring goods to them. It collects margins on each product and passes them to the trade and transport services that supply them. It sits inside Goods & services at every zoom, so these flows are listed, not drawn.
nodes.F_LREG: Compensation of regular wage and salaried employees, paid by industries to households (and a little to and from abroad).
nodes.F_LCAS: Compensation of casual workers, paid by industries to households.
nodes.F_MIXD: Mixed income: the earnings of household enterprises, such as farms and small shops, which mix pay for the owner's work with a return on their capital.
nodes.F_GOSC: Gross operating surplus: profits of companies and financial firms, governments' depreciation, and the surplus of owner-occupied and rented dwellings. It is gross, so it includes depreciation.
nodes.H_R1: Rural households in the poorest fifth by monthly spending per person. Income, spending and saving of this group are estimated by splitting national totals with survey keys.
nodes.H_R2: Rural households in the second fifth by monthly spending per person. The group's figures are estimated from national totals.
nodes.H_R3: Rural households in the middle fifth by monthly spending per person. The group's figures are estimated from national totals.
nodes.H_R4: Rural households in the fourth fifth by monthly spending per person. The group's figures are estimated from national totals.
nodes.H_R5: Rural households in the richest fifth by monthly spending per person. The group's figures are estimated from national totals; its saving rate looks implausibly low against the other rural groups (Checkpoint B).
nodes.H_U1: Urban households in the poorest fifth by monthly spending per person. The group's figures are estimated from national totals.
nodes.H_U2: Urban households in the second fifth by monthly spending per person. The group's figures are estimated from national totals.
nodes.H_U3: Urban households in the middle fifth by monthly spending per person. The group's figures are estimated from national totals.
nodes.H_U4: Urban households in the fourth fifth by monthly spending per person. The group's figures are estimated from national totals.
nodes.H_U5: Urban households in the richest fifth by monthly spending per person. The group's figures are estimated from national totals.
nodes.E_NFPU: Public non-financial corporations: government companies and departmental enterprises such as the Railways and Posts. Balancing moved several of their interest flows by amounts no source explains; those flows are flagged.
nodes.E_RBI: The Reserve Bank of India. It earns income on its foreign-exchange reserves and government securities and transfers its surplus to the Centre.
nodes.E_BANK: Banks and other deposit-taking corporations, including co-operative banks.
nodes.E_NBFC: NBFCs, housing finance companies, all-India financial institutions and financial auxiliaries.
nodes.E_INSP: Insurance corporations and provident and pension funds.
nodes.G_CEN: The Union government's current account, including central autonomous bodies and the Food Corporation of India.
nodes.G_STA: The current account of the States, Union Territories with legislatures and local bodies.
nodes.T_CGST: Central GST including UTGST, on a net basis after integrated GST is settled between the Centre and the States. Its level sits on the edge of a tolerance band around cash collections (Checkpoint B).
nodes.T_SGST: State GST on a net basis after integrated GST is settled.
nodes.T_GCES: The GST compensation cess. The Centre collects it but passes it on: as compensation grants to the States and to repay the back-to-back loans raised to pay them. Its level sits on the edge of a tolerance band around cash collections (Checkpoint B).
nodes.T_CUST: Customs duties on imports. Export duty is booked under other taxes on products.
nodes.T_UEXC: Union excise duties, mostly on petrol and diesel. Its level sits on the edge of a tolerance band around cash collections (Checkpoint B).
nodes.T_SVAT: State sales tax and VAT, which survives mainly on petroleum products and alcohol.
nodes.T_OPRT: Other taxes on products, including the States' motor-vehicle tax, export duty and the equalisation levy.
nodes.T_PSUB: Product subsidies, such as the fertiliser subsidy, recorded as negative taxes. The Centre and the States pay into this account and it lowers the prices in the product markets. Free food grain is not here: it is counted as government consumption.
nodes.T_PROD: Other taxes on production (stamp duty and registration fees, land revenue, property tax) less production subsidies, by industry.
nodes.T_PIT: Personal income tax and other direct taxes on households, including securities transaction tax. Part of it is paid by unincorporated firms treated as companies.
nodes.R_ROW: The rest of the world's current account with India: trade, incomes and transfers.
nodes.K_HH: Households' capital account: their saving and borrowing, and what they invest in homes and other fixed assets, inventories, valuables and financial assets.
nodes.K_RBI: The RBI's capital account, including changes in foreign-exchange reserves.
nodes.K_BANK: Banks' capital account: their saving, the loans they make, the securities they buy and the deposits they take.
nodes.K_NBFC: Capital account of NBFCs, housing finance companies and other lenders.
nodes.K_INSP: Capital account of insurers and pension funds.
nodes.K_MUTF: Mutual funds' capital account: the units they issue and what they invest in.
nodes.K_GCEN: The Centre's capital account: its (negative) saving, investment, capital grants and borrowing.
nodes.K_GSTA: The States' capital account: their saving, investment and borrowing.
nodes.K_ROW: The rest of the world's capital and financial account: India's current-account deficit, financed by foreign direct and portfolio investment, NRI deposits, external borrowing and changes in reserves.
nodes.K_DSTK: Change in inventories: goods produced but not yet sold or used, or stocks drawn down. Negative for some products.
nodes.I_DEPO: Deposits, including NRI deposits and certificates of deposit.
nodes.I_LOAN: Loans and advances, including external commercial borrowing and trade credit.
nodes.I_GSEC: Government securities of the Centre and the States, pooled in one account.
nodes.I_SSAV: Small savings schemes and public-account deposits.
nodes.I_CBND: Corporate debt securities and commercial paper.
nodes.I_EQTY: Shares and other equity, other than mutual fund units.
nodes.I_INPE: Insurance, pension and provident fund entitlements.
nodes.I_RESV: Reserve assets held by the RBI.
nodes.I_OTHR: Other accounts receivable and payable, and the per-sector residuals that reconcile national-accounts net lending with the flow of funds.
nodes.X_DISC: The discrepancy account. It holds the residuals described under Discrepancies and reconciliation items, each published or derived from published figures, held at those values.

links.PRDS--PROD: The value of everything Indian industries produce, at basic prices, paid from the market for each product to the industry that made it. This is gross output, not GDP: it also counts the inputs industries buy from each other, which is why it is larger than GDP. From the Supply-Use Tables.
links.PROD--PRDS: Intermediate consumption: what industries spend on goods and services used up in production, such as fuel, raw materials, transport and banking services. Output less these inputs is gross value added.
links.PROD--PRDS~neg: One tiny negative entry in the published Supply-Use Table (ownership of dwellings buying real estate services). It is shown reversed for completeness.
links.PROD--FACT: Industries' value added paid out to the factors of production: wages and salaries of regular and casual workers, the mixed income of the self-employed, and gross operating surplus (profits, rents and depreciation).
links.FACT--HH: Factor income that reaches households: wages and salaries, the mixed income of farms and household businesses, the imputed rent of owner-occupied homes, rent from tenants, and the surplus of household partnerships and non-profits. The totals follow national accounts; the split across the ten household groups is estimated with income gradients from an IFPRI social accounting matrix, because no household microdata were used.
links.HH--PRDS: What households, and the non-profits that serve them, spend on goods and services (private final consumption expenditure), including the rent owner-occupiers are deemed to pay themselves and the financial and insurance services they buy. The split across household groups is estimated from the household consumption survey, which captures well under half of national consumption; the method assumes the missing part is spread like the captured part.
links.SI--FINM: Financial assets acquired during the year: new deposits, purchases of government securities, shares and mutual fund units, insurance and pension contributions, and loans made. These are net flows in the year, not holdings. Who acquired what is estimated from RBI's flow of funds, re-matched to official totals where they exist. The money is pooled in each market, not traced from saver to borrower.
links.SI--FINM~neg: Where a sector's net acquisition of an instrument was negative, because it sold more than it bought, or a reconciliation residual is negative, the flow is drawn reversed. Examples are the RBI's net sales of government securities and negative 'other accounts' residuals.
links.FINM--SI: The other side of the financial markets: money reaching sectors when they take on liabilities. Banks accept deposits, governments issue securities, companies borrow and issue shares, households take loans. In every market, what is acquired equals what is incurred.
links.FINM--SI~neg: Where a sector repaid more of a liability than it took on, or a residual is negative, the flow is drawn reversed. One example is the States' repayment of the GST back-to-back loans, financed from the compensation cess.
links.SI--PRDS: Spending from capital accounts on goods and services: gross fixed capital formation (buildings, roads, machinery, software), the change in inventories, and valuables such as gold and silver. The totals follow national accounts; how investment is split among investing sectors is partly estimated.
links.SI--PRDS~neg: Products whose inventories were run down during the year: the change in stocks is negative, so the flow is drawn reversed.
links.PRDS--ROW: What India pays the rest of the world for imported goods and services. Imports of services are on the national-accounts basis; the difference from the balance of payments appears as a reconciliation item, under Discrepancies.
links.ROW--PRDS: What the rest of the world pays for India's exports of goods and services, including what foreign visitors spend in India.
links.HH--SI: Household gross saving: what households keep from their income after consumption, taxes, interest and transfers, whether held as money or invested in homes, gold or financial assets. The total is held to national accounts. Each group's saving is the residual of its own account, so the split is estimated; balancing raised every group's saving to reach the national total.
links.FACT--NFC: The gross operating surplus of public and private non-financial companies: what is left of their value added after paying their employees, before interest, dividends and taxes. It includes depreciation.
links.TAX--CEN: Union taxes passed from the tax accounts to the Centre: CGST including UTGST, the compensation cess, customs, Union excise, income tax and corporation tax, on the national-accounts accrual basis. This is before the Centre shares part of its tax pool with the States; that devolution is shown as a flow from the Centre to the States.
links.TAX--CEN~neg: Product and production subsidies paid by the Centre, such as the fertiliser subsidy. Subsidies are negative taxes, so this flow runs from the Centre into the subsidy accounts. Free food grain is not here; it is counted as government consumption.
links.PRDS--TAX: Taxes charged when goods and services are sold or imported: GST, Union excise, State VAT and excise, customs duties and other taxes on products. GST is recorded net, after the settlement of integrated GST.
links.PRDS--TAX~neg: Product subsidies, which lower what buyers pay, such as the fertiliser subsidy. They are negative taxes, so the flow runs from the subsidy account into the product markets. Some subsidies in the national accounts, on trade and on pesticides, have no payer in any budget: an open question (Checkpoint B).
links.NFC--SI: Gross saving of non-financial companies: their operating surplus and other income, less interest, dividends, taxes and other payments. It funds much of their investment.
links.FC--HH: What banks, insurers and pension funds pay households: interest on deposits, investment income attributed to insurance policyholders and to provident and pension fund members, non-life insurance claims, and income passed through mutual funds. How this income is split between sectors and across household groups is estimated.
links.STA--PRDS: What the States and local bodies spend on public services, such as the pay of teachers, police and health workers and the goods they buy, counted as government final consumption expenditure. Total government consumption follows national accounts; the Centre/State split is estimated.
links.CEN--STA: Money the Centre passes to the States: their share of Union taxes (devolution, as recommended by the Finance Commission), Finance Commission and scheme grants, GST compensation grants, the cess used to repay the GST back-to-back loans, and a little interest. Devolution matches the accounts exactly. Money released for schemes outside State treasuries is counted as a State receipt here, within a tolerance band.
links.TAX--STA: State taxes passed from the tax accounts to the States and local bodies: State GST, VAT and sales tax, State excise, stamp duties and registration fees, property tax, land revenue and other State taxes.
links.TAX--STA~neg: Product and production subsidies paid by the States and local bodies. Subsidies are negative taxes, so this flow runs from the States into the subsidy accounts. It is what remains of the national-accounts subsidy total after the Centre's share, and it is well above what the States' budgets report: an open question for the National Accounts Division (Checkpoint B).
links.FACT--FC: The gross operating surplus of financial corporations. Its total follows national accounts; the split among the RBI, banks, NBFCs and insurers is estimated.
links.NFC--FC: What companies pay financial firms: interest on loans and bonds, dividends and other distributed income, and non-life insurance premiums. Interest between sectors is estimated.
links.FC--SI: Gross saving of financial corporations. The total follows national accounts; its split among banks, NBFCs, insurers and the RBI is estimated, and two official sources disagree on it (Checkpoint B).
links.ROW--HH: Money sent home by Indians working abroad and other private transfers to households. The total follows the balance of payments; the split across household groups is estimated.
links.NFC--TAX: Corporation tax paid by non-financial companies, and the part of personal income tax paid by unincorporated firms that the accounts treat as companies.
links.CEN--PRDS: What the Union government spends on public services, including defence, administration and free food grain, counted as government final consumption expenditure. The Centre/State split of the total is estimated.
links.HH--TAX: Income tax and other direct taxes paid by households, such as professions tax. No open source gives income tax by household group, so that split is estimated.
links.STA--HH: What the States pay households: pensions of State employees, cash schemes such as support for women and old-age pensions, and interest on provident funds. The split across household groups is estimated.
links.NFC--HH: Dividends and other distributed income that companies pay households, directly or through mutual funds, and pensions paid by the Railways and Posts to their retired staff. The household share of distributed income is estimated with the old-base national-accounts structure.
links.HH--FC: What households pay financial firms: interest on loans, and non-life insurance premiums. Interest here is the pure interest; the banks' service margin is counted as consumption of financial services.
links.CEN--FC: Interest the Centre pays to banks, insurers, pension funds and the RBI on its securities and treasury bills. The split by holder is estimated.
links.CEN--HH: What the Centre pays households: interest on small savings, pensions, PM-KISAN payments to farm families (treated as a transfer, not a subsidy), other social security and cash transfers. The split across household groups is estimated.
links.HH--DISC: National accounts publish household disposable income, consumption and saving that do not add up; the gap is this residual. It is shown as its own flow and never folded into consumption or saving. The total is the published figure; its split across household groups is estimated in proportion to their gross income.
links.NFC--ROW: Income companies pay abroad: dividends to foreign direct investors, their reinvested earnings, interest on external borrowing, and portfolio income.
links.FC--NFC: What financial firms pay companies: interest on company deposits, non-life insurance claims, and dividends.
links.CEN--SI~neg: The Centre's negative gross saving (dissaving). In the year shown, the Union government's current spending was larger than its current receipts. The flow is drawn reversed: the Centre's capital account covers the gap, financed by borrowing. This is saving in the national-accounts sense, not the Budget's revenue deficit. General-government saving is official; its Centre/State split is estimated.
links.STA--FC: Interest the States pay to banks, insurers and other financial firms on State development loans and other borrowing. The split by holder is estimated.
links.DISC--SI: The saving-investment errors and omissions: investment less saving less net capital inflow, one residual derived from the published national accounts. Part of it is attributed to valuables that national accounts assign to no institutional sector, carried into the households' capital account (derived). The rest is spread over the capital accounts of companies and financial firms in proportion to their investment (estimated).
links.PROD--TAX: Other taxes on production paid by industries: stamp duty and registration fees, land revenue, property tax and similar taxes.
links.PROD--TAX~neg: Production subsidies: subsidies to industries that are not tied to the quantity of a product. They are negative production taxes, so the flow runs from the subsidy account to industries.
links.FACT--STA: The States' operating surplus, which for a government is the depreciation of its roads, buildings and other assets. The Centre/State split of this depreciation sits on the edge of a judgement band (Checkpoint B).
links.FC--ROW: Income financial firms pay abroad: interest on NRI deposits and external borrowing, dividends to foreign investors and their reinvested earnings.
links.DISC--ROW: A reconciliation item between national accounts and the balance of payments on imports of services (a CIF adjustment). It is an accounting adjustment, not money paid abroad.
links.ROW--SI: What the rest of the world earned from India on the current account and did not spend here: India's current-account deficit, which equals the rest of the world's saving in India and is financed by foreign investment and lending.
links.FC--TAX: Corporation tax paid by banks, NBFCs and insurers.
links.ROW--FC: Income from abroad received by financial firms, mostly the RBI's income on foreign-exchange reserves.
links.NFC--STA: What companies pay the States: mining royalties, interest on State loans, and dividends from State enterprises.
links.ROW--NFC: Income from abroad received by companies, such as dividends from their investments overseas.
links.FC--CEN: What financial firms pay the Centre: the RBI's surplus transfer (on the cash basis), dividends from public sector banks and LIC, and interest on government deposits.
links.NFC--CEN: What companies pay the Centre: dividends from public sector undertakings, spectrum and telecom licence fees, petroleum profit share and royalties, and interest on government loans.
links.FACT--CEN: The Centre's operating surplus, which for a government is the depreciation of its assets. The Centre/State split sits on the edge of a judgement band (Checkpoint B).
links.STA--SI: Gross saving of the States and local bodies. General-government saving is official; the Centre/State split is estimated.
links.HH--ROW: Private transfers that households send to people abroad.
links.ROW--FACT: Pay earned by residents working for non-resident employers.
links.CEN--NFC: What the Centre pays companies: grants to public sector undertakings and co-operatives, and interest on government securities they hold. The grants to public sector undertakings sit on the edge of a judgement band (Checkpoint B).
links.STA--CEN: Interest the States pay the Centre on loans from the Centre and from the National Small Savings Fund.
links.CEN--ROW: Interest the Centre pays abroad: on external assistance and on government securities held by foreign portfolio investors.
links.FACT--ROW: Pay earned in India by non-resident workers.
links.FC--STA: Interest financial firms pay the States on their deposits.
links.HH--STA: Mining royalties paid to the States by household enterprises.
links.STA--NFC: Interest the States pay companies on State securities they hold, directly or through mutual funds.
links.ROW--CEN: Income from abroad received by the Centre.
links.STA--ROW: Interest the States pay abroad, on State securities held by foreign portfolio investors.
links.HH--CEN: Interest households pay the Centre, such as on loans to government employees.
links.PRODUCERS--FACT: Industries' value added paid out to the factors of production: wages and salaries of regular and casual workers, the mixed income of the self-employed, and gross operating surplus (profits, rents and depreciation).
links.HH--PRODUCERS: What households, and the non-profits that serve them, spend on goods and services (private final consumption expenditure), including the rent owner-occupiers are deemed to pay themselves. The split across household groups is estimated from the household consumption survey, which captures well under half of national consumption.
links.SI--PRODUCERS: Investment spending: gross fixed capital formation (buildings, roads, machinery, software), the change in inventories, and valuables such as gold and silver.
links.SI--PRODUCERS~neg: Products whose inventories were run down during the year: the change in stocks is negative, so the flow is drawn reversed.
links.PRODUCERS--ROW: What India pays the rest of the world for imported goods and services. Imports of services are on the national-accounts basis; the difference from the balance of payments appears as a reconciliation item, under Discrepancies.
links.ROW--PRODUCERS: What the rest of the world pays for India's exports of goods and services, including what foreign visitors spend in India.
links.PRODUCERS--TAX: Taxes on products (GST, excise, VAT, customs and others) and other taxes on production (stamp duty, land revenue, property tax).
links.PRODUCERS--TAX~neg: Product and production subsidies, such as the fertiliser subsidy. They are negative taxes, so the flow runs from the subsidy accounts to producers.
links.STA--PRODUCERS: What the States and local bodies spend on public services, counted as government final consumption expenditure. The Centre/State split of the total is estimated.
links.CEN--PRODUCERS: What the Union government spends on public services, including defence and free food grain, counted as government final consumption expenditure. The Centre/State split of the total is estimated.

refs.P1: The make (supply) matrix: domestic output of each product by the industry that produced it, at basic prices, aggregated from MoSPI's Supply-Use Tables without changing any value.
refs.P2: Intermediate consumption: the inputs each industry buys, by product, at purchasers' prices, from the Supply-Use Tables.
refs.P3: Trade and transport services supplied into the margin account.
refs.P4: Trade and transport margins paid on each product.
refs.P5: Exports by product: goods valued free on board, and services, including what non-residents buy in India.
refs.P6: Imports by product, on the national-accounts basis.
refs.P7a: Taxes on products, split by tax type within each product.
refs.P9: Product subsidies by product (negative), from the Supply-Use Tables.
refs.P9a: Product subsidies split by the government that pays them, the Centre or the States.
refs.P10: Other taxes less subsidies on production, by industry.
refs.P10a: Production taxes and subsidies split between the Centre and the States.
refs.V1a: Compensation of employees by industry, split into regular and casual pay.
refs.V2a: Operating surplus and mixed income by industry, split into mixed income and gross operating surplus.
refs.V3: Compensation of employees received from the rest of the world.
refs.V4: Compensation of employees paid to non-residents.
refs.F1a: Labour income split across the ten household groups, using income gradients (estimated).
refs.F2: Mixed income (farm and non-farm) split across the ten household groups (estimated).
refs.F3a: The operating surplus of owner-occupied dwellings (imputed rent), by household group (estimated).
refs.F3b: Actual rent received by household landlords, by group (estimated).
refs.F3c: The operating surplus of household partnerships, trusts and non-profits serving households, by group (estimated).
refs.F4: Gross operating surplus of companies and general government, by national-accounts sector.
refs.F4a: The financial sector's gross operating surplus split across the RBI, banks, NBFCs and insurers (estimated).
refs.F4b: General government's gross operating surplus (its depreciation) split between the Centre and the States, within a judgement band.
refs.C1a: Household consumption of each product, split across the ten groups with shares from the household consumption survey (estimated).
refs.C4a: Housing services consumed by each household group: actual rent, imputed rent and government-provided housing (estimated).
refs.C4b: Financial intermediation and insurance service charges consumed by households (estimated by group).
refs.C4d: Out-of-pocket spending on health and education, by household group (estimated).
refs.C2a: Government final consumption by product, split between the Centre and the States (estimated split). Includes free food grain.
refs.I1a: Gross fixed capital formation by product and investing sector.
refs.I2: Gold and silver ornaments bought by households.
refs.I2a: Valuables that national accounts assign to no institutional sector, financed through the discrepancy account.
refs.I3a: Change in inventories by the sector that holds them.
refs.T1a: Union taxes converted to the national-accounts accrual concept and fitted to the product-tax totals of the Supply-Use Tables. Several sit on the edge of a tolerance band around cash collections.
refs.T2x: State taxes converted to the national-accounts accrual concept and fitted to the Supply-Use Tables.
refs.T2b: Uses of the GST compensation cess: compensation grants to the States, and cess applied to repay the GST back-to-back loans (treated as a current transfer for now).
refs.T3: Personal income tax, including securities transaction tax; part of it is paid by unincorporated firms treated as companies.
refs.T3a: Personal income tax by household group. No open source exists, so the split is estimated.
refs.T4a: Corporation tax by paying sector (estimated split; the public companies' share sits on the edge of a judgement band).
refs.R1: Tax devolution: the States' share of Union taxes, matched exactly to the accounts.
refs.R2: Grants from the Centre to the States, including money for schemes released outside State treasuries.
refs.R2k: Capital grants from the Centre to the States.
refs.R3: Interest paid by the Centre and the States, as published.
refs.R3a: Government interest split by the sector holding the debt (estimated).
refs.R4: Interest paid by financial firms on deposits and borrowing (national-accounts interest, net of the service margin).
refs.R5: Interest paid to financial firms on loans (national-accounts interest).
refs.R6: The RBI's surplus transfer to the Centre, on the cash basis.
refs.R7: Dividends from public sector undertakings, public sector banks and public insurers to governments.
refs.R7x: Other property income of governments: interest from non-government units and rents on natural resources such as mining and petroleum royalties and spectrum.
refs.R8: Dividends and other distributed income of companies to non-government holders.
refs.R8a: Interest, dividends and mutual fund income received by households, by group (estimated, partly with the old-base structure).
refs.R9c: Investment income attributed to insurance policyholders and provident and pension fund members (D44).
refs.R9d: Pensions paid by the Railways and Posts to their retired staff, within a judgement band.
refs.R9a: Government pensions by household group (estimated split).
refs.R10: Cash transfers to households, such as State schemes for women, old-age and widow pensions, scholarships and PM-KISAN.
refs.R11a: Remittances and other private transfers from abroad, by household group (estimated split).
refs.R12a: Private transfers sent abroad, by household group (estimated split).
refs.R13: Property income received from the rest of the world, by domestic recipient.
refs.R14: Property income paid to the rest of the world, by domestic payer.
refs.R14a: Reinvested earnings on foreign direct investment in India (D43), treated as paid to foreign investors.
refs.R17: Net non-life insurance premiums and claims.
refs.R18: Non-product subsidies and other current transfers to companies, such as grants to public sector undertakings and interest subvention.
refs.K1: Gross saving of public and private non-financial companies.
refs.K2a: Financial corporations' saving split among the RBI, banks, NBFCs and insurers (estimated).
refs.K3a: Government saving split between the Centre and the States (estimated split; the general-government total is official).
refs.K4a: Household saving by group, the residual of each group's account (estimated).
refs.K5: The rest of the world's saving in India, which equals India's current-account deficit.
refs.K6: Capital transfers and acquisitions of non-produced assets.
refs.K7: Acquisition of financial assets by sector and instrument.
refs.K8: Incurrence of liabilities by sector and instrument.
refs.K7b: Counterparty rule used where national accounts or the balance of payments replace flow-of-funds values.
refs.K7a: Household financial assets by instrument, from the new-base national accounts.
refs.K8a: Household borrowing, from the new-base national accounts.
refs.K8b: The rest of the world's financial account by instrument: direct and portfolio investment, external borrowing, NRI deposits, trade credit and reserves.
refs.K8c: The change in foreign-exchange reserves, on the balance-of-payments basis (excluding valuation changes).
refs.K8d: Net purchases of Central and State government securities, by holder (estimated from the flow of funds).
refs.K8e: The States' repayment of the GST back-to-back loans, financed from the compensation cess.
refs.K9: Per-sector reconciliation residual: national-accounts net lending less the flow-of-funds net financial transactions. It is large for banks and the States.
refs.K9b: The RBI surplus timing item: the accrued surplus payable compared with the cash actually transferred.
refs.D1: The household residual: national-accounts household disposable income less consumption less saving. Published total; split across household groups estimated.
refs.D2: Reconciliation between national accounts and the balance of payments on imports of services (CIF adjustment). Not money paid abroad.
refs.D3: The saving-investment errors and omissions (investment less saving less net capital inflow), derived from published national-accounts figures. One part is attributed to valuables with no institutional sector and carried into the households' capital account (derived); the rest is spread over companies and financial firms in proportion to their investment (estimated).
refs.D4: The GDP expenditure discrepancy. It is zero in 2023-24.

series.F01: What households and the non-profits that serve them spend on goods and services, from the national accounts. A derived series linked to the 2022-23 base is available for earlier years.
series.F02: What the Centre, States and local bodies spend on public services, from the national accounts.
series.F03: Investment in buildings, roads, machinery, equipment and software, excluding valuables. A derived series linked to the 2022-23 base is available.
series.F04: Gold and silver ornaments and other valuables bought, from the national accounts.
series.F05: Exports of goods. A derived linked series is available for earlier years.
series.F06: Exports of services, such as IT and business services. A derived linked series is available for earlier years.
series.F07: Imports of goods. A derived linked series is available for earlier years.
series.F08: Imports of services on the national-accounts basis, which differs from the balance of payments by a reconciliation item.
series.F09: Pay of employees in India, including employers' contributions.
series.F10: Gross operating surplus and mixed income: profits, rents, the earnings of the self-employed, and depreciation.
series.F11: Income Indians earn abroad less income foreigners earn in India. It is negative in most years, because India pays more investment income abroad than it receives.
series.F12: Taxes on products, including import duties.
series.F13: Product subsidies, shown as a positive amount paid.
series.F14: Central GST (including integrated GST not yet settled) and the compensation cess received by the Centre.
series.F15: State GST received by the States.
series.F16: Union excise duties, mostly on petroleum products.
series.F18: State sales tax and VAT. GST replaced most of it from 2017-18, which shows as a break.
series.F19: State excise duties, mostly on alcohol.
series.F20: Stamp duties and registration fees collected by the States.
series.F21: Corporation tax collected by the Centre.
series.F22: Personal income tax and other direct taxes on households, including securities transaction tax.
series.F23: The States' share of Union taxes, as recommended by successive Finance Commissions. The source changes in the series, which shows as a marker.
series.F24: Grants from the Centre to the States. The source changes in the series, which shows as a marker.
series.F25: Interest paid by the Union government. Only a short run of years is available, so it is shown as values, not a trend.
series.F27: Pensions paid by the Union government to its retired employees.
series.F28: Pensions paid by the States to their retired employees.
series.F29: The food subsidy. In the national accounts, free food grain is counted as government consumption.
series.F30: The fertiliser subsidy, shown as a positive amount paid.
series.F31: The RBI's surplus transferred to the Centre, on the cash basis.
series.F32: Saving of the Centre, the States and local bodies combined. Negative in every year of the series: governments together have spent more on current items than their current receipts (dissaving).
series.F33: Fixed investment by the Centre, the States and local bodies (public capex).
series.F34: New government securities issued by the Centre and the States, net of repayments. This is one way governments borrow; it is not the same as the Budget's fiscal deficit or national-accounts net borrowing.
series.F35: Household gross saving, in financial and physical assets.
series.F36: Households' acquisitions of financial assets: deposits, shares, insurance, pension funds and others.
series.F37: Households' new borrowing. A derived linked series is available for earlier years.
series.F38: Households' investment in homes and other physical assets, excluding valuables.
series.F39: Households' new deposits with banks and co-operative banks.
series.F40: Households' net purchases of shares, debentures and mutual fund units.
series.F41: Households' saving in insurance, provident and pension funds.
series.F42: Households' new borrowing from banks and co-operative banks.
series.F43: Remittances and other private transfers received from abroad, from the balance of payments.
series.F44: Private transfers sent abroad, from the balance of payments.
series.F45: Gross saving of private non-financial companies.
series.F46: Fixed investment of private non-financial companies (private capex).
series.F48: New liabilities taken on by non-financial companies: loans, bonds, shares and other liabilities. The map's figure is well above what companies report in RBI's flow of funds, because the two use different reporters; this is a known finding.
series.F49: India's current-account deficit, which equals the rest of the world's saving in India. In a few years it was a surplus, shown reversed.
series.F50: Investment income paid abroad, including the reinvested earnings of foreign direct investors.
series.F51: Net foreign direct investment into India.
series.F52: Net foreign portfolio investment in Indian shares and bonds. It can be negative.
series.F54: The increase in foreign-exchange reserves on the balance-of-payments basis. It can be negative.
series.M01: Gross domestic product at market prices: the value of all final goods and services produced in India in the year. It is the denominator for every share of GDP on this site.
series.M02: Gross value added at basic prices: GDP before taxes less subsidies on products.
series.M04: Imports of goods and services on the national-accounts basis.
series.M05: The reconciliation item between national-accounts and balance-of-payments imports of services (CIF adjustment).
series.M06: Imports of goods and services on the balance-of-payments basis, before the CIF adjustment.
series.M07: Taxes on products less product subsidies. In the top-flows view it is the ribbon from producers to government.
series.M08: Corporation tax plus personal income tax.
series.M09: Household financial assets acquired less liabilities incurred.
series.M10: The change in inventories. In some years stocks were run down, shown reversed.
series.M11: Private transfers received from abroad less those sent abroad.
series.M12: The household residual that national accounts publish but cannot allocate.
series.M13: Household gross disposable income: what households have to spend or save after taxes and transfers.
series.M14: The Union government's gross tax revenue, before devolution to the States.
series.M15: Property income paid by general government on the old national-accounts base. It is shown for reference and has no counterpart check in the map.
